name: The social contract and the creation of 'Leviathan'
plain_explanation: To escape the war of all against all, Hobbes imagines people agreeing among themselves (not with the ruler) to obey whatever sovereign the majority chooses. This creates the 'Commonwealth' or 'Leviathan,' an artificial person with the sovereign as its artificial soul; once created, the people's political role ends, since the covenant is not between citizens and ruler but among citizens themselves to obey the ruler.
precise_definition: Russell's account: 'It is supposed that a number of people come together and agree to choose a sovereign... which shall exercise authority over them and put an end to the universal war... The covenant is not, as afterwards in Locke and Rousseau, between the citizens and the ruling power; it is a covenant made by the citizens with each other to obey such ruling power as the majority shall choose. When they have chosen, their political power is at an end.' Russell stresses this 'covenant' is 'an explanatory myth,' not a claimed historical event.
why_it_mattered: This structural feature -- the contract binds citizens to each other, not to the sovereign -- is what makes the sovereign unbound by any contract while subjects remain bound, and thus grounds Hobbes's denial of any right of rebellion.
historical_origin: Central argument of Part II of Leviathan (1651).
examples: 'Covenants, without the sword, are but words' -- Hobbes's insistence that the covenant requires an enforcing power to be effective, which Russell notes 'President Wilson unfortunately forgot'
competing_positions: Locke's and Rousseau's later social-contract theories, in which the contract binds citizens and ruler to each other
influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly contrasted by Russell with Locke and Rousseau, whose contract theories reverse this structure.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: The commonwealth's creation is explicitly likened to God's creation of man ('Let Us make man').
